verses.translation_literal: For the choirmaster, a psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the one who leads the singing: a psalm, David's.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a stage direction, not a line to be spoken in character. In the Hebrew Bible the heading is verse 1, so every verse below is one higher than the KJV, which prints the title unnumbered. Treat it as the cue card handed to the lead singer: the poem that follows belongs to the temple's musical repertoire and was meant to be performed.

The KJV 'chief Musician' is a fair guess at a rare word, but the Hebrew is a participle of the root n-tz-ch, 'to lead, to excel, to oversee', and the other renderings in the packet split on whether he is a conductor, a choirmaster or an 'Overseer' (YLT). 'Of David' (ledavid) can mean by, for or belonging to David; the preposition does not settle authorship.

philological_notes.note: A participle with the preposition l-: 'to/for the one who leads (or oversees)'. Appears in the heading of over fifty psalms; its exact duty (conducting, supervising the temple singers, or the performance itself) is not stated.
A 'psalm' is a piece sung or played, from the root z-m-r, 'to make music, to pluck'. The word names the genre, not the theme.

verses.translation_literal: The heavens [are] recounting [the] glory of God, and [the] work of his hands the expanse [is] declaring.
verses.translation_dramatic: The heavens are telling it, on and on: the glory of God. And the work of his hands, the great hammered vault above, makes it known.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two parallel lines, and both verbs are participles: the telling is not an event but a state, going on right now. Hold the first word, 'the heavens', wide and open, as if looking up. The speakers here are not people; the sky itself is the witness.

The KJV's 'declare' and 'sheweth' blur two different verbs. Hebrew says mesaprim, 'are counting out, recounting', the root of 'scribe' and 'number', and maggid, 'is reporting', the verb for bringing news. The KJV's 'firmament' comes from the Latin firmamentum, a 'firm' thing; the Hebrew raqia' is the sheet beaten thin, as a smith hammers metal (Gen 1:6), so the sky is a worked object. 'Handywork' is archaic for 'work of his hands'. And the name is El, the old short word for God, not Elohim, which sets the psalm's first half in the vocabulary of nature and power; the covenant name YHWH waits until verse 8.

There is also an unspoken polemic. In Israel's world the sun, moon and stars were gods; here they are exhibits, the 'work of his hands', and their only job is to talk about someone else.

philological_notes.note: Pi'el participle: 'recounting, counting out'. The root yields 'book, scribe, number, tell'; the sky is writing a report and also counting.

'The expanse', literally what is beaten out (cf. 'hammered' gold plating, Num 17:4). Radak and Rashi identify it with the sky in which God set the stars (Gen 1:17); Ibn Ezra takes it as the air. Malbim distinguishes it from 'the heavens' as the zone of rain.

verses.translation_literal: Day to day it pours forth speech, and night to night it shows forth knowledge.
verses.translation_dramatic: Day hands it to day, a spring that never stops spilling words; and night whispers it on to night, a knowledge passed hand to hand in the dark.
verses.directors_commentary:
Relay, not a recital. Each day passes the news to the next, each night to the next night, and the two halves of the line are the two shifts of the sky: one shouts in light, the other speaks in the dark. Play the day line open and bright, the night line lower and slower.

The Hebrew verb for the day's speech, yabbia', is the verb of a spring bubbling up (the same root as 'spring', nove'a), so the KJV's tidy 'uttereth' loses the image of water that cannot be held back. 'Omer, 'speech', is rare and poetic. Night 'shows forth' (yechaveh) 'knowledge' (da'at): the Aramaic cognate is the ordinary word for 'to declare', and Rashi glosses it simply as 'telling'. In a world with no light pollution, the nights were the sky's most eloquent hour, and the word 'knowledge' fits an audience who navigated and kept the calendar by it.

The doubled 'day to day' and 'night to night' in the Hebrew are meant to echo each other; the KJV keeps the idiom but prints 'unto' for the preposition l-, which sounds like address rather than handing on.

philological_notes.note: 'Pours forth, bubbles up', as a spring. Menachem (via Rashi) reads it as a flowing fountain; Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as plain 'speaks' (cf. Ps 59:8, 119:171).
'Declares, shows forth', an Aramaic-flavored verb of announcing, as in Job 32:10.

verses.translation_literal: There is no speech and there are no words, without their voice being heard.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet there is no speech. No words. No sound that any ear has caught. Their voice is never heard.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn: after two lines of pouring and telling, the verse takes the sound away. This is a pause the director should let stand. The heavens are eloquent and mute at once; the 'speech' is something you see, not hear. Radak and Metzudat David say it plainly: they do not speak in words, but what a person sees in them makes him tell of God.

The KJV, 'There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard', adds the word 'where' (it is not in the Hebrew) and turns the line into the opposite claim: that wherever there is language, the sky is heard. The older Greek version was read that way, and the ASV and BBE keep the plain reading ('their voice is not heard'). The Hebrew has just beli nishma' qolam, 'without voice-heard', and works with either; the dramatic layer takes the silence because the verse before has just shown the telling to be a pouring that nobody hears. 'Language' is also the KJV's softening of devarim, which is simply 'words, things'.

philological_notes.note: 'Without [their] voice being heard.' beli is a negative that can introduce a clause ('with no ...'); the Hebrew has no 'where'. Ibn Ezra and Radak take the heavens to have no mouth; Meiri also records a view that the line means no word, however whispered, is unheard.

verses.translation_literal: In all the earth their line has gone out, and at the end of the world their words; for the sun he has set a tent in them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Yet across the whole earth their reach has gone out, their words to the world's far edge. And among them, for the sun, he pitched a tent.
verses.directors_commentary:
From silence to reach: the voiceless message has gone everywhere. Keep the pace steady, then slow for the last clause, which begins the sun's section. 'The end of the world' is the rim of the known earth, as an audience of shepherds and farmers would picture it.

Qaw, 'line', is the crux. It is a measuring line or cord (Isa 28:17, 1 Kings 7:23), as Radak and Metzudat Zion read it, a plumb-line of construction; Ibn Ezra reads it as 'their writing'. The Septuagint reads 'sound', hence Romans 10:18, which is why the older translations vary; the KJV and ASV keep 'line', and the BBE too. Mille-hem, 'their words', is the plain word of speech, matched against 'line', so the verse sets measuring-cord and word in one frame: the sky is both a built structure and a message.

Then the sun. The KJV's 'tabernacle' is the wrong word: 'ohel is an ordinary herdsman's tent, the one you pitch for a night and strike in the morning. Nothing here makes the sun a god. In Mesopotamia the sun was the god Shamash, judge and all-seeing; here God simply sets him a tent. Rashi, citing the Tanchuma, has the sun placed in a sheath.

philological_notes.note: 'Their line': a measuring cord or construction line (so Radak, Metzudat Zion), or a line of writing (Ibn Ezra). Rashi: the line of the heavens stretched across the earth.
A tent. Not the sanctuary word mishkan, which the KJV's 'tabernacle' evokes.
The inhabited world, poetic. Malbim: the inhabited part of the earth.

verses.translation_literal: And it, like a bridegroom going out from his canopy, rejoices like a warrior to run a path.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he comes, the sun, like a bridegroom stepping out of the wedding chamber, and glad as a champion who sets out to run his road.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sun has an entrance, and this is it: joy at dawn. Play it as a double picture. First the bridegroom, radiant, stepping out of his canopy after the wedding week; then the champion who runs because he is strong enough to love the run. Neither image is gentle: both are power that is glad to be used.

Huppah, which the KJV and ASV call 'chamber', is the bridal canopy or covered bower, the place where the marriage is consummated; the BBE's 'bride-tent' captures the physical setting best. The verb yasis, 'rejoices', is the one for exulting; the 'runner' is a gibbor, 'a strong man, a warrior', not an athlete in a modern race. And the KJV's 'race' misleads: 'orach is a road or path, the sun's daily course, not a contest. Rashi says: every morning. Radak: all rejoice at the sight, as at the bridegroom.

The verb is a grammatical surprise: 'he' (hu') has no name, because the sun was named only in the previous verse. A good reader keeps the pause just there.

philological_notes.note: The bridal canopy or room; the word later gives the Jewish wedding canopy its name. In Joel 2:16 the bride goes out from her chuppah.
'Rejoices, exults'; Radak compares the warhorse that 'exults in strength' in Job 39:21, so the joy is the joy of force.
A path or way, as a traveled road; not a contest.

verses.translation_literal: From the end of the heavens [is] its going out, and its circuit [is] upon their ends, and there is none hidden from its heat.
verses.translation_dramatic: From one edge of the sky it goes out; to the other edge it circles. And nothing, nothing at all, hides from its heat.
verses.directors_commentary:
Trace the sun's day with your voice: sunrise at one rim (mitzo'o, 'its going out'), the long arc across, the far rim at evening. The last clause is the weight. You cannot hide from this thing, and the line sets that against the earlier silence: heard by nobody, felt by everybody.

The KJV's 'circuit' is fine for tequfah, from the root 'to go around'; the same word names the turning of the year (Exod 34:22), and Radak notes the sun's yearly drift south in winter, north in summer. The KJV's 'nothing hid from the heat thereof' is accurate; chammah is the sun's heat, a poetic name for the sun itself elsewhere in the Bible. In Palestine's summer there is truly no shade to count on, and a shelterless worker, a shepherd, a soldier in the open lived by that. Radak: one can hide from the sun's light but not from its heat, which reaches even the inner rooms. In Mesopotamia the sun was the judge who saw everything; here, the sun sees nothing, it only warms.

philological_notes.note: 'Its circuit, its going around', from the verb meaning 'to go around' (Isa 29:1); the word is also the technical term for the equinox and solstice turning points.
'From its heat'. Radak: the verse says 'heat', not 'light', since a person may hide from the light but not from the heat.

verses.translation_literal: The instruction of YHWH [is] whole, restoring life; the testimony of YHWH [is] reliable, making wise the simple.
verses.translation_dramatic: The teaching of the LORD is whole, with nothing missing; it brings a person back to life. The LORD's witness can be trusted; it makes the untaught wise.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from the sun that nobody can hide from to a second, quieter proclamation, and the actors should feel the change of register: the heat of verse 7 gives way to a list. Six names for God's word follow in verses 8-10, and YHWH is spoken in each of the six clauses: instruction, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear, judgments. After verse 10 the name drops out for the whole of the prayer in verses 11-14 and returns only once more, in the last verse (15), 'YHWH, my rock'. So the ear hears six strokes of the name, then a human voice that has to speak without it until the final line. Rashi counts the six names against the six orders of the Mishnah; the verse itself gives the six names, which is enough to play.

The KJV's 'law' is narrower than torah, which is 'instruction', from the verb for pointing the way; Radak lists the torah of the leper, of the Nazirite, of the woman after childbirth, all of them rules for how something is done. Its 'perfect' is acceptable for tamim ('whole, with nothing missing', the word for an unblemished offering). 'Converting the soul' is archaic and misleading: meshivat nefesh is 'bringing back life'. Nefesh is the throat, the breath, the living self, not a ghost inside a body, and shuv is 'turn back, return', the verb for coming home or reviving the faint (Ruth 4:15 uses the same root for a restorer of life). In the ancient Near East the sun god Shamash was also the god of justice and legal order, and the psalm has just shown the sun as a servant; it now gives the role of lawgiver and healer to YHWH's word. 'Sure' for ne'emanah is weaker than the Hebrew, which comes from the root of 'amen' and means 'dependable, load-bearing'. The 'simple', peti, is not a fool: he is the naive, open, unformed person who can still be taught, and Proverbs addresses him as a pupil.

philological_notes.note: 'Instruction', from the verb 'to direct, to teach'. Radak lists the torah of the leper, of the Nazirite and so on, and shows that torah can mean the 'form of a rule'. The KJV's 'law' is narrower than the word.

'Restoring life', literally 'bringing the nefesh back'. Rashi reads it as turning a person from the ways of death to the ways of life; Metzudat Zion links the verb to Ruth 4:15, 'a restorer of life'. Nefesh is the living self, not a soul apart from the body, so 'converting' misleads.
The simple, naive person, open to being shaped for good or ill; not a fool in the sense of kesil. The text says the testimony makes such a person wise.

verses.translation_literal: The precepts of YHWH [are] straight, making glad [the] heart; the commandment of YHWH [is] clear, lighting up [the] eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD's charges run straight, and they make the heart glad. The LORD's command is clear and clean, and it puts light back in the eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The list continues: each line pairs a name for God's word with a quality and with what it does to a person. Here the effects are bodily, heart and eyes. Keep the rhythm of the pairs steady, and let the last phrase land bright.

The KJV's 'statutes' misses piqqudim, which are 'things entrusted, charges, orders', from the verb 'to appoint, to deposit' (Radak compares Gen 41:36, the 'deposit' of grain). 'Right' for yesharim is 'straight', the opposite of crooked. 'Pure' for barah is 'clean, clear', related to bar, 'grain cleared of chaff'; Rashi glosses it simply 'bright as noon'. And the KJV's 'enlightening the eyes' is a bit abstract: me'irat 'enayim is 'making the eyes light up'. In 1 Samuel 14:27 Jonathan tastes honey and his eyes 'light up', a close parallel in imagery for the next verse's honey, though that is my own association, not a source's. The heart in Hebrew is also the seat of thought, so 'making glad the heart' is mind and mood together.

philological_notes.note: 'Precepts, charges', literally what is deposited with someone. Radak and Meiri derive it from piqqadon, 'a deposit', which fits the sense of things set aside in the heart.
'Clear, clean, bright'. Rashi: 'noon-bright'; Metzudat Zion: from the idea of clear and clean.

verses.translation_literal: The fear of YHWH [is] clean, standing for ever; the judgments of YHWH [are] truth, they are righteous together.
verses.translation_dramatic: Reverence for the LORD is clean, and it stands for ever. The LORD's judgments are true: every one of them, together, just.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last two names of the series, fear and judgments, and the last two qualities, standing and truth. This is the close of the list, so let the voice settle into finality, especially on 'together'.

The KJV's 'fear of the Lord' is accurate but needs the Hebrew's weight: yir'ah is awe, reverence before something that can destroy you, and in the Bible it is not a shaking terror but the working posture of a worshiper. 'Clean' (tehorah) is the vocabulary of ritual purity: a clean animal, a cleansed leper. 'Enduring for ever' translates a participle, 'standing', so the image is a thing that remains on its feet when everything else is gone. 'The judgments' (mishpatim) are rulings, case law, what a judge decides. The KJV's 'true and righteous altogether' crams in an extra 'and'; Hebrew says 'truth, they are righteous together': 'emet, the noun, then a verb, tzadequ, 'they have proved just', then yachdav, 'as one'. Radak's reading: no ruling contradicts another, unlike the sun that is seen at one horizon and absent at the other.

philological_notes.note: 'Fear, awe, reverence'. Radak ties it to the things a person does in secret, from awe of God alone, not fear of other people; Ibn Ezra reads it as the prohibitions.
A perfect verb: 'they have proved righteous', together, as one. Radak: no judgment contradicts another; Metzudat David: unlike the sun, which seems to contradict itself between horizons.

verses.translation_literal: The desirable [ones], more than gold, and more than much refined gold, and sweet, more than honey and [the] drippings of honeycombs.
verses.translation_dramatic: More to be longed for than gold, than heaps of the purest gold; and sweeter than honey, than the honey that drips from the comb.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the senses: first the eye (gold), then the tongue (honey). The verse is a pair of comparisons, each stacked: 'gold, and even much refined gold'; 'honey, and even the dripping of the comb'. Build the line upward, and let 'sweet' be tasted.

In an ancient economy gold was the only wealth that did not rot, and honey the only sweetener most people ever had, so the two comparisons are the most valuable thing and the most delicious thing in the world. Paz is refined or fine gold, and the KJV's 'fine gold' is fine. The loss is in the second line: nofet tzufim is not 'the honeycomb' but 'the drippings of honeycombs', honey that runs from the comb unpressed, the first and finest, as the Hebrew 'drip' root (Prov 5:3) shows; the ASV and BBE see this, the KJV flattens it. 'To be desired' is one passive participle, 'the desirable ones', the same root as 'covet' in the tenth commandment, now turned toward the good.

philological_notes.note: 'Drippings of honeycombs', honey that drips from the comb. Rashi and Metzudat Zion both connect nofet to dripping (Prov 5:3, Song 4:11); tzuf is the honeycomb (Prov 16:24).
Refined, pure gold. Radak records the view that it means precious stones, which the Hebrew does not support elsewhere; the verse just means the best gold.

verses.translation_literal: Also your servant is warned by them; in keeping them [is] great consequence.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, your servant, am warned by them; and in keeping them there is a great reward.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm moves from the sky to the speaker. 'Your servant' is the first person to appear, and the first 'you': a direct address to God. Lower the volume and bring the voice close. The singer is no longer a bystander admiring the cosmos; he is someone who stands under these words.

The KJV's 'by them is thy servant warned' is right; nizhar can also mean 'is made careful, is enlightened', and 'servant' is 'eved, a bondservant, a slave of a king, which in the royal court is a title of honor, not shame. The harder word is 'eqev, which the KJV makes 'reward'. It is literally 'heel', and so what comes at the heel: the result, the consequence. Rashi cites Genesis 26:5, 'because (eqev) Abraham listened to my voice', and the sense 'end, outcome'. Radak: the reward is the 'end of the deed', as the heel is the end of the body. So 'reward' is a reasonable word for it, but the Hebrew keeps a richer picture of a consequence that follows behind the keeping. The adjective rav, 'great', is the same word that closed verse 11's 'much gold'.

philological_notes.note: Nif'al of zhr: 'is warned, is careful, is made watchful'. Radak takes it as the servant's own watchfulness: he is among those who are careful of the commands.

Literally 'heel', so what comes at the heel: consequence, result, reward. Rashi compares Gen 26:5 and gives the second reading 'end'. Metzudat Zion and Radak: reward as the end of the deed, as the heel is the end of the body.

verses.translation_literal: Errors, who will discern [them]? From hidden [ones] clear me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Errors: who can see them? From the hidden ones, clear me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops. After five verses of praise in the third person, the speaker stops describing and speaks in the first person, and the verse is only two clauses, one question and one plea, with no verb of motion and no ornament. The question has no answer, because it is not meant to have one: the speaker means that nobody can see all his own errors. Play it as a short, honest breath, not as a speech.

The KJV's 'secret faults' is a little off. Nistarot are 'hidden ones', things hidden from the speaker himself, and the KJV makes them sound like private vices; Rashi reads them as sins that were hidden from him, done unknowingly, and Radak says the speaker asks not to be punished for them. 'Cleanse' also changes the picture: naqqeni is from the root of acquittal and innocence (naqah, as in Exodus 34:7, 'he will by no means clear the guilty'), so the plea is a courtroom request, 'hold me innocent of them', where the KJV and Webster hear water and soap. Shegi'ot, 'errors', occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; it is related to shagah, 'to go astray', the stray step of someone walking in good intent.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun for 'errors, slips', used only here in the Hebrew Bible. It is related to the verb shagah, 'to stray, go astray'. Ibn Ezra comments on the spelling, with its aleph. Radak and Meiri read it as including both unwitting acts and unknown sins.
From the root of acquittal and being free of guilt, so 'clear me' or 'hold me innocent'. Radak glosses the request as 'do not punish me for the hidden ones, but acquit me of them'.

verses.translation_literal: Also from presumptuous [ones] hold back your servant; let them not rule over me. Then I will be blameless, and I will be cleared from great transgression.
verses.translation_dramatic: And more than that: hold back your servant from the proud and defiant. Let them never rule over me. Then I shall stand whole before you, blameless, cleared of the great rebellion.
verses.directors_commentary:
The plea widens. Verse 13 asked pardon for what the speaker cannot see; verse 14 asks protection from what he can see all too well, the zedim, the arrogant and presumptuous. The speaker calls himself 'your servant' (ʿebed) for the second time, and the word matters: a servant who is ruled by someone else's will cannot serve his master, so the plea is about whose rule he lives under. Mashal b-, 'to rule over', is the verb of kings and masters. 'He shall rule over you' (Genesis 3:16) and 'will you indeed rule over us?' (Genesis 37:8) use the same verb, and the preposition bet there, as here, means 'over', not 'in'.

The KJV adds a word the Hebrew does not have: 'presumptuous sins' makes zedim an abstract noun, and the old verse reads as if the speaker fears only acts. Zedim is a plain plural, 'the presumptuous, the insolent', and it may name the proud people as easily as their proud deeds; Radak and Meiri read it as 'presumptuous deeds'. The KJV also gives 'upright' and 'innocent' for eitam and niqqeti. The first is 'I shall be blameless, whole' (the root of tamim, the same word as 'whole' in verse 8, so the psalm ends with the speaker asking to be what the instruction is) and the second is the acquittal word again from verse 13. 'The great transgression' is Hebrew 'great pesha', rebellion against a master (the word used in 2 Kings 3:7 for Moab's revolt, as Rashi notes); there is no definite article, and it is not a single named sin.

Radak supplies the best stage direction: the speaker will try, and God must also hold him back, as God told Abimelech in Genesis 20:6, 'I also held you back from sinning against me.' The prayer is not 'I will be good', it is 'keep me from being ruled by what I could not resist alone'.

philological_notes.note: Plural of zed, 'insolent, presumptuous'. The word is used for arrogant people or for arrogant acts. Radak and Meiri compare it with the noun pattern of 'resh' and 'osher' in Proverbs 30:8, which shows the word can stand as a noun for a quality. The KJV's 'sins' is an addition.
'I shall be blameless, whole'. The yod after the aleph is unusual; Radak and Meiri read it as a variant of 'etam, and Ibn Ezra calls it a strange word. It shares its root with tamim in verse 8.

Rebellion, deliberate breach against a master or ruler. Rashi cites 2 Kings 3:7, 'the king of Moab has rebelled (pasha') against me'. Radak places it above zadon, wilful sin, as the worst: the one who despises the commandment itself.

verses.translation_literal: Let them be for acceptance, the sayings of my mouth and the murmuring of my heart, before you, YHWH, my rock and my redeemer.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the words I speak aloud, and the thoughts I turn over in the silence of my heart, be welcome in your presence. O LORD, my rock, my redeemer.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the closing line of the psalm, and it should be spoken slowly and almost whispered. After the sun, the heavens and the Torah, the voice narrows to one man standing before God with his mouth and his heart. Let the last two words come as a settling, like a hand placed on solid stone.

The KJV 'be acceptable in thy sight' uses a familiar phrase, but the Hebrew is more concrete: yihyu le-ratzon, 'let them be for acceptance', the word used for the favor with which a sacrifice is received. The psalmist offers his words as an offering and asks that it be welcomed. 'Sight' (KJV, ASV) translates lefanekha, which is literally 'before your face'. The pair 'mouth' and 'heart' is deliberate, and Radak explains it: the words are what was spoken, the hegyon is what was thought but never said. The noun hegyon comes from the verb hagah, 'to murmur, mutter, ponder', the low sound of a man talking to himself. The KJV 'meditation' is good, though 'murmuring' keeps the physical sound of the thought. Radak adds that people think many things they do not say, so the psalmist asks that even these be welcome.

The closing names matter. In the KJV 'LORD' (capitals) marks the divine name YHWH. 'Rock' (tzur) is a title with a concrete picture: a cliff or crag where a hunted man hides, a standard image in the Psalms. The KJV renders it 'my strength' and so loses the picture; BBE does the same. Radak glosses it as the strong one in whom he trusts, which supports the sense, but the image is a rock. 'Redeemer' (go'el) is a family word: the kinsman who buys back a relative from debt or slavery or avenges his blood. In the world of the psalm, this is the one who comes to claim the sinner who cannot clear himself. Radak says the redemption is from errors and presumptuous acts, which ties the last line to the plea that came just before. Ibn Ezra hears relief: with God as rock and redeemer, the presumptuous cannot win.

philological_notes.note: From hagah, to murmur or ponder. The word names inner speech, thought not yet said aloud. Radak and Metzudat David both read it as what is in the heart and cannot be put into words.
'My rock', a title for God as the high, unmoving refuge. Radak glosses it as 'my strong one', so the KJV 'strength' is an old reading, but it drops the image of the rock itself.
'My redeemer', a participle of ga'al, the kinsman who buys back or defends a relative. Radak understands it here as redemption from the errors and presumptuous sins of the verses before.
